claims.claim: Cyril of Jerusalem was born around 315 and served as bishop of Jerusalem from about 348 until his death in 386.
He wrote the Epistula ad Constantium imperatorem in May 351 to report an apparition of a luminous cross in the sky over Jerusalem.
The letter was addressed to Emperor Constantius II during the emperor’s military conflict with the usurper Magnentius.
Cyril used the letter to declare his loyalty to Constantius and to portray the emperor as a devout Christian ruler.
In the letter Cyril links the heavenly cross to the eschatological ‘sign of the Son of Man’ described in Matthew 24:30.
The vision described a massive cross of light that stretched from the holy Golgotha to the Mount of Olives, was seen by the whole city for many hours, and outshone the sun.
Cyril wrote the letter in order to attract imperial attention to Jerusalem and to enhance the city’s ecclesiastical status against the rival see of Caesarea.
The episode of the cross‑vision and Cyril’s letter became a celebrated motif in Byzantine historiography and liturgy, commemorated on May 7 in the Eastern tradition.
